# Agency Types Explained: Full-Service to Specialist

Source: https://lowob.com/research/agency-types-field-guide/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

Even large advertisers now do most routine work in-house and buy agencies for capacity and specialist skill. Agencies specialise, and the specialisation determines what you get. The main types are full-service, performance, media, creative, PR and specialist agencies, each paid differently and good at different things. The buying pattern of large advertisers points the same way: in the ANA's 2023 survey, 82% of members had an in-house agency and 92% still used outside agencies, mainly for capacity or skills they lacked. Most small and mid-sized companies need one partner who owns distribution and brings in specialists, not a full-service agency.

"We should hire an agency" is the start of a decision, not the end of one. Agencies specialize, and the specialization determines what you will get. The US Census Bureau's Service Annual Survey shows the scale of the market: in 2022, employer advertising agencies earned about $64 billion, public relations agencies about $20 billion, and other advertising services about $18 billion. Within those totals sit businesses with very different economics.

## The main types

**Full-service agencies** offer strategy, creative, media, digital, and often PR under one roof. The appeal is one relationship and one invoice. The trade-off is that every function is staffed to an average, and the agency's economics favor the services with the best margin, which is rarely the one you most need. Best for companies with broad needs and a budget large enough to be a priority client.

**Performance agencies** run paid acquisition, typically on the large self-serve platforms, and are judged on cost per outcome. They are fast, numerate, and dependent on the platforms working for your category. If the platforms will not carry your product, a performance agency has little to sell you. Paid by retainer, percentage of spend, or a fee plus a performance bonus.

**Media agencies** plan and buy media across channels, including programmatic, television, out-of-home, and audio. Their value is in access, negotiation, and measurement at scale. Historically paid a percentage of spend, which is the incentive problem covered in [Percent of spend is a conflict of interest with a logo on it](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/). Best for large budgets where buying power matters.

**Creative agencies** make the work: brand identity, campaigns, film, design. They are paid by project or retainer, and their output is judged on craft and effect. They do not usually distribute what they make, and a creative agency with no distribution partner produces beautiful things nobody sees.

**PR agencies** earn coverage and manage reputation. They are paid on monthly retainers and are judged, imperfectly, on placements. Good for companies with news, a credible spokesperson, and a story a journalist would want regardless of the pitch. Poor value for companies with none of those.

**Specialist agencies** do one thing: affiliate management, influencer programs, app-store optimization, search, community, a single vertical. They are usually better at that thing than a full-service shop and worse at everything adjacent. Paid by retainer or project, sometimes by performance.

| Type | Sells | Usually paid by | Good fit | Poor fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Full-service | Breadth under one contract | Retainer, often blended with media fees | Broad needs, budget large enough to be a priority client | A company that mainly needs one function done well |
| Performance | Paid acquisition at a target cost | Retainer, % of spend, or fee plus bonus | Categories the self-serve platforms carry openly | Restricted categories; slow, considered purchases |
| Media | Planning, buying power, measurement | % of spend, increasingly fees | Large multi-channel budgets | Small budgets where buying power is irrelevant |
| Creative | Brand and campaign work | Project or retainer | A brand problem with distribution already in place | No plan for who will see the work |
| PR | Earned coverage and reputation | Monthly retainer | Real news and a credible spokesperson | No news and no story |
| Specialist | Depth in one channel or vertical | Retainer, project, sometimes performance | A defined gap with a clear owner | Expecting them to cover adjacent channels |

## What the evidence says about incentives

Two of the types carry incentive problems that are documented rather than anecdotal.

**Media.** In 2016 the ANA commissioned K2 Intelligence to investigate US media buying. The report found cash rebates paid to agencies on the basis of client spend, often unknown to the advertiser, and principal-based buying in which agencies bought inventory and resold it to clients at mark-ups of roughly 30% to 90%. Some advertiser contracts had not been reviewed in up to ten years. The ANA's recommendation was to re-examine contracts and extend audit rights to the holding company, so advertisers can follow the money. None of this means a given media agency behaves badly. It means the contract, not trust, decides what you get.

**Performance.** Performance pay is most common in media disciplines. A 2026 study of 69 multinational advertisers by the World Federation of Advertisers and Agency Mania Solutions, reported by VideoWeek, found labour-plus-performance models had grown from 9% to 21% over 15 years. Yet for most respondents performance pay was still under 20% of total agency compensation. Performance agencies talk about outcomes; the bulk of the fee usually still pays for time or spend.

## How to tell them apart in a pitch

Ask three questions and listen for where the energy goes.

**Where does most of your revenue come from?** The answer tells you what the agency is actually built to sell.

**Show me a client whose category the platforms restricted.** If the answer is a blank look, the agency is built for the crowded auction. Restrictions are specific and change often. Google, for example, permits crypto exchange and wallet ads only in listed countries, only for advertisers it has certified, and only where they meet local registration rules; it added Argentina in September 2025. An agency that has worked under rules like these will describe them without being prompted. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers the wider picture.

**What would you not do for us, and who would you bring in instead?** A confident answer signals a specialist who knows their edges. A "we do everything" answer signals a generalist who will subcontract quietly.

> A "we do everything" answer signals a generalist who will subcontract quietly.

## The mix most companies actually need

Small and mid-sized companies rarely need a full-service agency. They need one partner who owns distribution and can bring in specialists for the parts that do not scale in-house: PR when there is news, creative when the brand needs work, a clipping or creator specialist when the program calls for it.

Large advertisers have arrived at a similar shape by a different route. The ANA's 2023 in-house agency survey of 162 members found in-house teams handled an average of 61% of company work, and 65% had moved established work from outside agencies to in-house in the previous three years. Work still went outside for two reasons: the in-house team was too busy, or the company lacked a specialised capability. Gartner's 2025 CMO survey points the same way, with 39% of marketing leaders planning to cut agency budgets. The pattern is a close core with specialists at the edge, which is the model our piece on [the modular GTM team](https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/) sets out.

That is the model we run: distribution built and run directly, with PR, creative production, and specialist networks packaged from partners rather than staffed permanently. It keeps the core work close and the peripheral work with people who do it every day.

The same logic applies to the partners themselves. When specialists are brought in, someone needs to own the brief, the handoffs and the measure, or the company ends up integrating the work itself. Our piece on [the commercial system](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) covers the shared definitions and records that make that ownership possible, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to judge what each channel returns.

Agencies are specialists wearing general names. Find out where an agency's revenue comes from, whether it has worked in a restricted category, and what it would not do, before you find out the expensive way.

## lowob takeaways

- **Hire the type, not the label.** Each agency type is built to sell different work and is paid differently.
- **Read media and performance contracts closely.** The incentive problems in both are documented, and the contract decides what you get.
- **Test for category experience.** Ask to see a client the platforms restricted.
- **Keep the core close.** One partner owning distribution, with specialists at the edge, fits most mid-sized firms better than full-service.
